title: Application Isolation and Sandboxing
summary: Isolation runs code inside a boundary that limits what it can read, write and reach. That boundary may be a virtual machine, a container, a browser sandbox, a restricted operating system job, or a dedicated analysis environment. Enforcement comes from several layers: hypervisor separation, kernel namespaces and control groups, mandatory access control profiles, system call filtering, restricted tokens or job objects, and network rules that keep a sandbox away from production. The aim is damage control rather than prevention, because the code may still be malicious and simply unable to touch anything valuable. Evidence includes sandbox policy definitions, container security settings, blocked system calls, file writes landing in temporary overlay paths, and network denials from the isolated workload. Practical failures are broad mount points, privileged containers, shared host directories, and outbound access that turns a sandbox into a launch pad.

beginner.definition: Isolation means running a program inside a small, closed box. The program can work normally inside the box, but it cannot touch the rest of your computer. A sandbox is one kind of box, and people often use it to open risky files. If the code is harmful, the damage stays inside the box.
beginner.whyItMatters: You cannot read every file or check every download by hand. Isolation lets you handle risky material without trusting it. If harmful code escapes the box, it can reach your files, your network and your other systems. That is why the walls of the box matter more than the label on it. Weak settings, such as allowing full disk access, make the protection useless.
howItWorks: You choose a boundary, such as a virtual machine, a container or a browser sandbox.
The program starts inside that boundary with only the files and tools it needs.
The host system limits what the program may read, write and connect to.
Any attempt to step outside the boundary is blocked and usually written to a log.
When the program stops, you throw the whole environment away and start fresh.
You review the logs to learn what the sample tried to do.
beginner.example: Picture a hospital isolation room. Nurses can treat a patient with a serious infection, but the room has its own air supply, its own door and its own waste route. The patient still receives care, yet the infection cannot spread through the ward. Staff follow strict rules about what leaves the room. A sandbox is that room for software, because the program runs and can be studied while its reach stops at the door. If the door is propped open, the whole ward is at risk.
takeaways: Isolation limits damage, it does not decide whether code is safe.
The boundary is only as strong as its settings, so avoid full access.
Log what the isolated code tries to do, then rebuild the environment.

objectives: Explain what isolation and sandboxing protect and what they do not.
Compare virtual machines, containers and browser sandboxes in simple terms.
Identify settings that weaken a sandbox boundary.
Describe how logs from an isolated environment support later analysis.
Explain why disposable environments reduce long term risk.
